notes.front: What is GitHub Advanced Security (GHAS)?
notes.back: GitHub's paid security products, GitHub Code Security and GitHub Secret Protection, which add security features beyond those in every plan.
notes.explanation: Some features, such as the dependency graph and Dependabot alerts, come with all plans; the others need one of these products.
notes.example: Like buying an alarm system on top of the locks every house already has: the dependency graph comes free, code scanning of a private repository does not.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Advanced Security”, “About GitHub Advanced Security products”
notes.evidence: Some of these are included in all plans, such as dependency graph and {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot_alerts %}. Other security features require you to purchase one of {% data variables.product.github %}'s {% data variables.product.prodname_AS %} products:

notes.front: What is secret scanning?
notes.back: A GitHub feature that automatically detects credentials, such as keys and passwords, committed to repositories, so you can secure them before they are exploited.
notes.explanation: Hardcoded credentials committed to a repository become targets for unauthorised access.
notes.example: Like a metal detector sweeping the whole beach, including sand dug up years ago, for keys someone dropped.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Secret scanning”
notes.evidence: When credentials like API keys and passwords are committed to repositories as hardcoded secrets, they become targets for unauthorized access. {% data variables.product.prodname_secret_scanning_caps %} automatically detects credential leaks so you can secure them before they're exploited.

notes.front: What are validity checks in secret scanning?
notes.back: Checks that verify whether a detected secret is still active, so you can prioritise which secrets to remediate first.
notes.explanation: When they are enabled, secret scanning may contact the service that issued the secret to find out whether it has been revoked.
notes.example: Like ringing the bank to ask whether a lost card still works before deciding how urgently to cancel it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Secret scanning”, “About validity checks”
notes.evidence: Validity checks help you prioritize which secrets to remediate first by verifying whether a detected secret is still active. When you enable validity checks, {% data variables.product.prodname_secret_scanning %} may contact the secret's issuing service to determine if the credential has been revoked.

notes.front: What is push protection?
notes.back: A secret scanning feature that blocks pushes containing secrets before they reach the repository, instead of alerting after the leak.
notes.explanation: It is designed to stop hardcoded credentials, such as secrets or tokens, from ever being pushed.
notes.example: Like a letterbox that refuses an envelope with a house key taped inside, rather than a note later saying the key went missing.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Push protection”, “What is push protection?”
notes.evidence: Rather than alerting you to credential leaks after the fact, push protection blocks pushes that contain secrets _before_ they reach your repository.

notes.front: What is code scanning?
notes.back: A GitHub feature for finding security vulnerabilities and errors in the code of your project on GitHub.
notes.explanation: It looks at your project's own code, rather than its dependencies or its secrets.
notes.example: Like a proofreader who checks the whole manuscript for dangerous errors, then checks each new page before it is added.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning”
notes.evidence: You can use {% data variables.product.prodname_code_scanning %} to find security vulnerabilities and errors in the code for your project on {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %}.

notes.front: What is CodeQL?
notes.back: A programming language and tools, from GitHub, that treat code like data to find potential vulnerabilities; its results appear as code scanning alerts.
notes.explanation: It was created to make it easier to find vulnerabilities with greater confidence than traditional static analysers.
notes.example: Like loading a whole city map into a database and asking "which streets lead from the river to the bank vault?"
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning with CodeQL”, “About CodeQL”
notes.evidence: {% data variables.product.prodname_codeql %} is a programming language and associated tools that treat code like data. It was created explicitly to make it easier to analyze code and find potential vulnerabilities in your code with greater confidence than traditional static analyzers.

notes.front: What is dependency review?
notes.back: A pull request view showing which dependencies changed, including indirect ones in lock files, and whether any added or updated ones have known vulnerabilities.
notes.explanation: Checking it before merging, and changing flagged dependencies, keeps vulnerabilities out of the project.
notes.example: Like a customs officer checking every new crate on a ship, including the boxes packed inside other boxes, before it docks.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependency review”, “About dependency review”
notes.evidence: The dependency review includes details of changes to indirect dependencies in lock files, and it tells you if any of the added or updated dependencies contain known vulnerabilities.

notes.front: What are Dependabot alerts?
notes.back: Notifications that your code depends on a package with a known security vulnerability, so you can upgrade to a secure version.
notes.explanation: Depending on vulnerable packages can make you a target for attackers seeking access to your code, data, customers or contributors.
notes.example: Like a product-recall letter telling you the kettle you already own has a faulty part.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependabot alerts”
notes.evidence: {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot_alerts %} notify you about vulnerable dependencies so you can upgrade to secure versions and protect your project.

notes.front: What are Dependabot security updates?
notes.back: Automatic pull requests from Dependabot that try to fix a vulnerable dependency when a Dependabot alert is raised for it.
notes.explanation: They make it easier to fix vulnerable dependencies in your repository.
notes.example: Like a recall letter that arrives with the replacement part already in the box, ready for you to fit.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependabot security updates”, “About Dependabot security updates”
notes.evidence: If you enable {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot_security_updates %}, when a {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot %} alert is raised for a vulnerable dependency in the dependency graph of your repository, {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot %} automatically tries to fix it.

notes.front: What are Dependabot version updates?
notes.back: Dependabot pull requests that keep your repository up to date with the latest releases of the packages and applications it depends on.
notes.explanation: Dependabot raises a pull request to update the manifest whenever it identifies an outdated dependency.
notes.example: Like a magazine subscription that posts each new edition, not only corrections to errors.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependabot version updates”, “About Dependabot version updates”
notes.evidence: You can use it to ensure that your repository automatically keeps up with the latest releases of the packages and applications it depends on.

notes.front: What is open source licence compliance on GitHub?
notes.back: A feature that tracks the licences of your dependencies and enforces a licence policy, catching nonconforming dependencies before changes are merged.
notes.explanation: You can use it to reduce legal and operational risk from the open source software in your supply chain.
notes.example: Like a publisher checking that every quoted passage in a book has permission before it goes to print.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About open source license compliance”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: Open source license compliance helps you **track dependency licenses** and **enforce policy** for the open source software in your supply chain. You can use license compliance to reduce legal and operational risk, catching nonconforming dependencies **before** changes are merged.

notes.front: What is GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps?
notes.back: A product that adds GitHub Advanced Security's security features, such as secret, dependency and code scanning, to Azure Repos.
notes.explanation: It is available only for Azure DevOps Services, and only for code Git repositories.
notes.example: Like a security firm fitting the same alarm system it sells for offices into a different landlord’s building.
introduces: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps adds GitHub Advanced Security's suite of security features to Azure Repos and includes the following features:
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: What is Defender for Cloud DevOps security?
notes.back: The part of Microsoft Defender for Cloud that gives security teams one console for protecting code and resources across Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitLab.
notes.explanation: Its recommendations can be linked with other cloud security insights, so teams can decide which code problems to fix first.
notes.example: Like a head of security who reads the alarm reports from three different buildings on one screen.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Overview of Microsoft Defender for Cloud DevOps security”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the GitHub Advanced Security integration with Defender for Cloud?
notes.back: A link between GitHub repositories and the cloud workloads built from them, so teams can fix first the vulnerabilities that reach production.
notes.explanation: Engineers can then fix those findings without leaving GitHub.
notes.example: Like linking each car on the road back to its factory batch, so a recall starts with the cars actually being driven.
introduces: GitHub Advanced Security integration with Defender for Cloud
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “What is GitHub Advanced Security integration with Microsoft Defender for Cloud?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is secret sprawl?
notes.back: The uncontrolled spread of credentials across repositories.
notes.explanation: Scanning the whole history of every branch helps you spot it before it becomes a security risk.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Secret scanning”, “How secret scanning protects your code”
notes.evidence: This helps you identify secret sprawl, the uncontrolled proliferation of credentials across repositories, before it becomes a security risk.

notes.front: Secret scanning raises an alert for a database password in a repository. What should you do first?
notes.choices:
A) Rotate the password at once
B) Rewrite the Git history first, then decide
C) Close the alert as a false positive
D) Make the repository private
notes.back: A) Rotate the password at once
notes.choicesExplained: B is slow and often unnecessary once the credential is revoked. C leaves a real credential usable. D does not revoke a password others may already have.
notes.explanation: GitHub says to rotate the affected credential immediately; rewriting history is time-intensive and often unnecessary once the credential is revoked.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Secret scanning”, “Secret scanning alerts and remediation”
notes.evidence: When you receive an alert, rotate the affected credential immediately to prevent unauthorized access. While you can also remove secrets from your Git history, this is time-intensive and often unnecessary if you've already revoked the credential.

notes.evidence: **Custom patterns.** Define your own regular expressions to detect organization-specific secrets that aren't covered by default patterns.

notes.explanation: Once enabled, GitHub immediately generates the dependency graph and creates alerts.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependabot alerts”, “Who can enable alerts?”
notes.evidence: Repository administrators and organization owners can enable {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot_alerts %} for their repositories

notes.front: Which version does a Dependabot security update pull request move a vulnerable dependency to?
notes.back: The minimum version that includes the patch; the pull request is linked to the Dependabot alert.
notes.explanation: Dependabot first checks it can upgrade without disrupting the dependency graph.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependabot security updates”, “About Dependabot security updates”
notes.evidence: raises a pull request to update the dependency to the minimum version that includes the patch and links the pull request to the {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot %} alert, or reports an error on the alert.

notes.front: A repository has a Dependabot alert for a package found only in its full dependency graph, not in any manifest or lock file. Why is no security update pull request raised?
notes.choices:
A) Alerts and security updates are the same thing
B) Security updates need a `dependabot.yml` file to run at all
C) Security updates are triggered only for dependencies specified in a manifest or lock file
D) Security updates run only on archived repositories
notes.back: C) Security updates are triggered only for dependencies specified in a manifest or lock file
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: a `dependabot.yml` file is optional and customises Dependabot behaviour. A is wrong: an alert reports, an update raises a pull request with a fix. D is wrong: Dependabot does not scan archived repositories.
notes.explanation: You see an alert for every vulnerable dependency in the graph, but security updates only for those in a manifest or lock file.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependabot security updates”, “About Dependabot security updates”
notes.evidence: You will see a {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot %} alert for every vulnerable dependency identified in your full dependency graph. However, security updates are triggered only for dependencies that are specified in a manifest or lock file.

notes.front: What do grouped Dependabot security updates do, and what will they never group together?
notes.back: Raise one pull request per package ecosystem group; they never mix ecosystems or combine security updates with version updates.
notes.explanation: Grouping reduces the number of pull requests.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependabot security updates”, “About grouped security updates”
notes.evidence: {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot %} **will not** group dependencies from different package ecosystems together, and it **will not** group security updates with version updates.

notes.front: You enable Dependabot version updates by checking a {{c1::`dependabot.yml`}} configuration file into the repository.
notes.explanation: The file tells Dependabot where the manifests are and how to maintain the dependencies.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependabot version updates”, “About Dependabot version updates”
notes.evidence: You enable {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot_version_updates %} by checking a `dependabot.yml` configuration file into your repository.

notes.front: A team wants its workflow files to keep using the latest versions of the actions and reusable workflows they reference. What should it enable?
notes.choices:
A) Dependabot alerts
B) Dependabot version updates for GitHub Actions
C) Secret scanning
D) Dependency review
notes.back: B) Dependabot version updates for GitHub Actions
notes.choicesExplained: A reports vulnerabilities but raises no update pull requests. D shows dependency changes in a pull request. C looks for credentials.
notes.explanation: Dependabot then checks each action reference and each called reusable workflow and raises pull requests to update them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependabot version updates”, “Updates for actions”
notes.evidence: When you enable {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot_version_updates %} for {% data variables.product.prodname_actions %}, {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot %} will help ensure that references to actions in a repository's _workflow.yml_ file and reusable workflows used inside workflows are kept up to date.

notes.front: Dependabot security updates versus version updates: what triggers each pull request?
notes.back: Security updates: a Dependabot alert for a vulnerable dependency. Version updates: any dependency Dependabot detects as outdated.
notes.explanation: Version updates are a related feature that keeps the manifest on the latest version.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependabot security updates”, “About Dependabot security updates”
notes.evidence: You can enable a related feature, {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot_version_updates %}, so that {% data variables.product.prodname_dependabot %} raises pull requests to update the manifest to the latest version of the dependency, whenever it detects an outdated dependency.

notes.front: How do you specify the licences a licence policy allows?
notes.back: From a built-in list, or, for a licence not listed, by adding its standard licence identifier by hand.
notes.explanation: The enterprise policy controls which licences dependencies may use.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About open source license compliance”, “How license policy works”
notes.evidence: You can specify licenses from either a built-in list or, if a license is not listed, by manually adding a SPDX license identifier.

notes.front: What enforces an open source licence policy, and at which scopes?
notes.back: Rulesets, defined at enterprise, organisation or repository scope.
notes.explanation: Exceptions can be added when an Enterprise Open Source License Manager approves them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About open source license compliance”, “How license policy works”
notes.evidence: Your policy is enforced by rulesets that can be defined at the enterprise, organization, and repository scope.

notes.front: A team wants licence checks to annotate pull requests for a month without blocking any merges. Which ruleset mode should use the "Requires license compliance results before merging" condition?
notes.choices:
A) Active
B) Dependabot security updates
C) Secret scanning custom patterns
D) Evaluate
notes.back: D) Evaluate
notes.choicesExplained: A blocks pull requests that introduce noncompliant dependencies until violations are resolved. C detects secrets, not licences. B fixes vulnerable dependencies and does not check licences.
notes.explanation: An Evaluate mode ruleset runs the checks and annotates the pull request without blocking; Active mode blocks noncompliant pull requests.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About open source license compliance”, “How pull request enforcement works”
notes.evidence: An **Evaluate** mode ruleset with that condition will run license checks and annotate the pull request, but not block merges.

notes.front: What are two features of the bundled GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps?
notes.back: Any two of: secret scanning push protection, secret scanning repo scanning, dependency scanning, code scanning.
notes.explanation: These mirror the GitHub Advanced Security suite, added to Azure Repos.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: * Secret Scanning push protection: check if code pushes include commits that expose secrets such as credentials * Secret Scanning repo scanning: scan your repository and look for exposed secrets that were committed accidentally
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: Under which two standalone products is GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps also available?
notes.back: GitHub Secret Protection for Azure DevOps and GitHub Code Security for Azure DevOps.
notes.explanation: The split lets you enable the right level of protection per repository.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps is available as GitHub Secret Protection for Azure DevOps and GitHub Code Security for Azure DevOps.
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: At which levels can you enable Advanced Security in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: Organisation, project or repository.
notes.explanation: You must enable it before you can use the scanning tools and see their results.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps”, “Enable GitHub Advanced Security” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can enable Advanced Security at the organization, project, or repository level. To access each of the scanning tools and results, you need to first enable Advanced Security.
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: A project administrator selects Enable all for Advanced Security. A week later a new repository is created in the project without it. Why?
notes.choices:
A) New repositories must wait for the weekly scan
B) Advanced Security works only on the default repository
C) Enable all covers only existing repositories; automatic enablement for new ones is a separate setting
D) Billing has not begun for the organisation
notes.back: C) Enable all covers only existing repositories; automatic enablement for new ones is a separate setting
notes.choicesExplained: A confuses enablement with the CodeQL default setup schedule. B is invented. D is wrong: Begin billing activated the existing repositories already.
notes.explanation: The automatic setting for new repositories must be selected independently of Enable all.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps”, “Enable GitHub Advanced Security” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This setting is separate from the **Enable all** action and must be selected independently.
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: In Azure DevOps, which secret tool finds secrets from historical commits, and which only checks pushes made after it is enabled?
notes.back: Repository-level secret scanning finds historical secrets; push protection evaluates only pushes after enablement.
notes.explanation: Both switch on automatically with Advanced Security or Secret Protection.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps”, “Set up secret scanning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Push protection only evaluates pushes that occur after the feature is enabled. Repository-level secret scanning detects and alerts on existing secrets, including those from historical commits.
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: When a resource needs paired credentials, when does Azure DevOps secret scanning raise an alert?
notes.back: Only when both parts of the pair are found in the same file.
notes.explanation: Pair matching also reduces false positives, since both parts are needed to reach the resource.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up secret scanning”, “About secret scanning alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If access to a resource requires paired credentials, secret scanning creates an alert only when both parts of the pair are detected in the same file.
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: Azure DevOps secret scanning flags a storage key in a repository. What is the recommended remediation?
notes.choices:
A) Lower the alert severity to medium
B) Delete the branch that contains it
C) Wait for autofix to close the alert
D) Invalidate the key, create a new one, and store it securely, for example in Azure Key Vault
notes.back: D) Invalidate the key, create a new one, and store it securely, for example in Azure Key Vault
notes.choicesExplained: B does not revoke the key, and the alert covers all history. C is wrong: secret alerts have no autofix. A is not possible: all secret scanning alerts are critical.
notes.explanation: Microsoft says to invalidate the exposed credential, replace it, and store the new one so it is not pushed back into code.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up secret scanning”, “About secret scanning alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To remediate exposed secrets, invalidate the exposed credential and create a new one in its place. The newly created secret should then be stored securely in a way that doesn't directly push it back into the code. For example, the secret could be stored in Azure Key Vault.

notes.front: In GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps, every secret scanning alert has the severity {{c1::critical}}.
notes.explanation: Any exposed credential is potentially an opportunity for a malicious actor.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up secret scanning”, “Alert details” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | Severity | All secret scanning alerts are set as critical. Any exposed credential is potentially an opportunity for a malicious actor. |
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: To bypass Azure DevOps push protection for a secret you believe is safe, include {{c1::`skip-secret-scanning:true`}} in the commit message.
notes.explanation: An alert is still generated once the secret is pushed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up secret scanning”, “Push a blocked secret” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Include the string `skip-secret-scanning:true` in your commit message. Even if you bypass push protection, a secret scanning alert is generated in the alert UX once the secret gets pushed.

notes.front: Azure DevOps push protection rejects a push because the secret is in your most recent commit. What should you do?
notes.choices:
A) Remove the secret, run `git commit --amend`, and push again
B) Add a new commit that deletes the secret and push both commits
C) Disable Advanced Security for the repository
D) Run an interactive rebase from the first commit in the repository
notes.back: A) Remove the secret, run `git commit --amend`, and push again
notes.choicesExplained: B leaves the secret in the earlier commit, which is still pushed. C removes protection instead of the secret. D is the approach for secrets further back in history, and starts from the wrong commit.
notes.explanation: For a secret in the immediate previous commit, Microsoft says to amend the commit; an interactive rebase is for older commits.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up secret scanning”, “What to do if your push was blocked” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If the secret was added in your immediate previous commit, amend the commit and create a new commit: 1. Remove the secret from your code. 2. Commit the changes by using `git commit --amend` 3. Push your changes again.

notes.front: Advanced Security is enabled on a repository, but no dependency scanning alerts ever appear. What is missing?
notes.choices:
A) Push protection must be switched off
B) A `dependabot.yml` file in the repository
C) A weekly CodeQL schedule
D) A pipeline running `AdvancedSecurity-Dependency-Scanning@1`, or dependency scanning default setup
notes.back: D) A pipeline running `AdvancedSecurity-Dependency-Scanning@1`, or dependency scanning default setup
notes.choicesExplained: A is unrelated to dependency scanning. B configures Dependabot on GitHub, not Azure DevOps. C schedules code scanning, not dependency scanning.
notes.explanation: Enabling Advanced Security or Code Security does not run dependency scanning by itself.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up dependency scanning”, “Learn about dependency scanning detection” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Dependency scanning requires running a pipeline configured with the `AdvancedSecurity-Dependency-Scanning@1` task or running a pipeline in a repository with dependency scanning default setup enabled. > Enabling Advanced Security or Code Security doesn't execute dependency scanning automatically.
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: When does an Azure DevOps dependency scanning alert close automatically?
notes.back: When the vulnerable component is no longer detected in the latest build of any pipeline that has the dependency scanning task.
notes.explanation: Closed alerts are found with the State filter.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up dependency scanning”, “Learn about dependency scanning alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: An alert’s state is automatically updated to `Closed` when the vulnerable component is no longer detected in the latest build for any pipelines where the dependency scanning task is installed.
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: For code scanning with advanced setup in Azure Pipelines, the order is `AdvancedSecurity-Codeql-Init@1`, then your custom build steps, then {{c1::`AdvancedSecurity-Codeql-Analyze@1`}}.
notes.explanation: The initialise task is also where you name the languages to analyse.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up code scanning”, “Advanced setup for code scanning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Add the tasks in the following order: 1. Advanced Security Initialize CodeQL ([AdvancedSecurity-Codeql-Init@1](/azure/devops/pipelines/tasks/reference/advanced-security-codeql-init-v1)) 1. Your custom build steps 1. Advanced Security Perform CodeQL Analysis

notes.front: How often does CodeQL default setup in Azure DevOps run, and what happens when you first enable it for an organisation or project?
notes.back: Weekly; an initial scan is queued at once for all affected repositories.
notes.explanation: Results begin appearing without waiting for the next scheduled run.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps”, “Set up code scanning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To generate alerts, default setup runs on a weekly schedule. Any detected vulnerabilities are displayed in the Advanced Security tab. When you enable CodeQL default setup at the organization or project level, an initial scan run is automatically queued for all affected repositories
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: What are two languages that CodeQL default setup in Azure DevOps cannot scan?
notes.back: Go and Swift.
notes.explanation: You scan them with advanced setup.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up code scanning”, “About code scanning setup types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Go and Swift aren't currently supported by default setup. To scan these languages, use advanced setup.

notes.front: Repositories using CodeQL default setup need access to a private network. Which agent pool option should the organisation choose?
notes.choices:
A) The Azure Pipelines pool of Microsoft-hosted agents
B) Any pool: default setup never builds code
C) A self-hosted agent pool
D) A GitHub-hosted runner
notes.back: C) A self-hosted agent pool
notes.choicesExplained: A uses Microsoft-hosted agents, which lack the private network. B ignores the need for network access. D is a GitHub Actions runner, not an Azure DevOps agent pool option here.
notes.explanation: Microsoft suggests a self-hosted pool when repositories need private networks, specific build tools or other resources not on hosted agents.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up code scanning”, “Agent pool” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Self-hosted agent pools** — uses your own agents. Select a self-hosted pool if your repositories require access to private networks, specific build tools, or other resources not available on hosted agents.

notes.front: A team must run CodeQL on release branches as well as the default branch in Azure DevOps. Which setup does it need?
notes.choices:
A) Neither: CodeQL scans only pull requests
B) Default setup
C) Either: both scan every branch
D) Advanced setup
notes.back: D) Advanced setup
notes.choicesExplained: B scans the default branch only. C is wrong because default setup covers only the default branch. A is wrong: advanced setup scans any branch that triggers the pipeline.
notes.explanation: Default setup scans the default branch only; advanced setup scans any branch that triggers the pipeline.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up code scanning”, “About code scanning setup types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | **Branch coverage** | Scans default branch only | Scans any branch that triggers the pipeline |

notes.front: CodeQL default setup versus advanced setup in Azure DevOps: how do they handle build steps?
notes.back: Default setup has no custom build steps and uses `none` build mode; advanced setup gives full control of build steps for compiled languages.
notes.explanation: This is one of the listed differences between the setups.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Set up code scanning”, “About code scanning setup types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | **Build customization** | No custom build steps — uses `none` build mode | Full control over build steps for compiled languages |

notes.front: A team with many old high-severity alerts wants to stop new critical or high vulnerabilities being merged without first fixing the old ones. Which status check should it require?
notes.choices:
A) `AdvancedSecurity/AllHighAndCritical`
B) `AdvancedSecurity/NewHighAndCritical`
C) Push protection
D) A Dependabot version update
notes.back: B) `AdvancedSecurity/NewHighAndCritical`
notes.choicesExplained: A requires every critical and high alert across the repository to be resolved first. C blocks secrets at push, not vulnerabilities at merge. D is a GitHub feature that updates dependencies.
notes.explanation: This check blocks new vulnerabilities without requiring all existing ones to be fixed first.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps”, “Set up pull request status checks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Block on new critical and high vulnerabilities** (`AdvancedSecurity/NewHighAndCritical`): Use this check to prevent new vulnerabilities from being introduced without requiring all existing vulnerabilities to be fixed first.

notes.front: For Advanced Security billing, a committer is active if they appear in a push made within the last {{c1::90}} days.
notes.explanation: Each active committer to at least one enabled repository uses one licence.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Advanced Security billing” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A committer is considered active if they're present in a push made within the last 90 days, regardless of when they originally committed.
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: Repository X, in one Azure DevOps organisation, has 25 active committers; repository Y, in another, has 15; 5 people commit to both. Both organisations use one Azure subscription. How many Advanced Security licences are used?
notes.choicesExplained: A counts the shared committers twice. B subtracts the shared committers twice. C counts only repository X.
notes.explanation: Active committers are deduplicated across an Azure subscription, so the 5 shared people count once: 25 + 15 − 5.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Advanced Security billing” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Active committers are deduplicated across an Azure subscription. Users can contribute to multiple repositories or organizations and only get counted once, as long as those organizations are associated with the same Azure subscription.
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: How and where is GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps billed?
notes.back: Monthly, directly to the Azure subscription linked to the Azure DevOps organisation, from daily active-committer charges.
notes.explanation: The count is the total active committers per day across your organisations.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Advanced Security billing” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Advanced Security gets billed monthly and directly to the Azure subscription associated with your Azure DevOps organization. Daily charges emit to your Azure subscription based off of the total number of active committers per day across your organizations.
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: An existing customer asks to move from bundled Advanced Security to the standalone products. At what level does the migration happen, and can it be undone?
notes.back: At Azure subscription level, covering all its organisations; it is irreversible.
notes.explanation: The request is made through a support ticket in the Azure portal.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Advanced Security billing”, “Migrating to standalone experiences” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This operation is completed at the subscription level, so all organizations tied to the provided Azure subscriptions will be migrataed to see the standalone Secret Protection and Code Security proudcts. This is an irreversible request.
uses: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: Which kinds of scan findings does the Defender for Cloud DevOps security console summarise?
notes.back: Code, secrets, dependency and infrastructure-as-code findings, grouped by severity and type.
notes.explanation: Security administrators see them across all connected DevOps environments.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Overview of Microsoft Defender for Cloud DevOps security”, “Understand your DevOps security”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where in the Azure portal do you start connecting a GitHub organisation to Defender for Cloud?
notes.back: Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > Add environment > GitHub.
notes.explanation: You then authorise access and install the Defender for Cloud GitHub application.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Quick Start: Connect your GitHub Environment to Microsoft Defender for Cloud”, “Connect your GitHub environment”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An engineer is Contributor on the Azure subscription but only a member of the GitHub organisation. What else is needed to connect the organisation to Defender for Cloud?
notes.choices:
A) Project Collection Administrators membership
B) Nothing more
C) Organisation owner rights in GitHub
D) A classic personal access token
notes.back: C) Organisation owner rights in GitHub
notes.choicesExplained: A is an Azure DevOps group, needed for Azure DevOps connectors. B misses the GitHub side. D is not the listed requirement; access is granted by installing a GitHub App.
notes.explanation: The required permissions include Contributor on the subscription to create the connector and owner of the GitHub organisation.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Quick Start: Connect your GitHub Environment to Microsoft Defender for Cloud”, “Availability”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A user with Stakeholder access is in Project Collection Administrators and tries to connect the Azure DevOps organisation to Defender for Cloud. What stops it?
notes.choices:
A) The organisation must first enable GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps
B) Azure DevOps cannot connect to Defender for Cloud
C) The user also needs Basic (or Basic + Test Plans) access level
D) The user must be a GitHub organisation owner
notes.back: C) The user also needs Basic (or Basic + Test Plans) access level
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: there is a native Azure DevOps connector. A is not a listed prerequisite. D applies to GitHub connectors.
notes.explanation: Microsoft says both Project Collection Administrator rights and Basic access are required, and that Stakeholder access is not enough.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Connect Azure DevOps environments to Defender for Cloud”, “Availability”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Whose identity does Defender for Cloud use for operations in a connected Azure DevOps organisation, and what does Microsoft recommend?
notes.back: The account that authorised the connector; Microsoft recommends a dedicated service account.
notes.explanation: Actions such as pull request annotations appear as that account in audit logs.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Connect Azure DevOps environments to Defender for Cloud”, “How Defender for Cloud uses your identity”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the DevOps inventory table in Defender for Cloud, what does an advanced security status of "Partially enabled" mean?
notes.back: Some advanced security features, such as code scanning, are not turned on for that resource.
notes.explanation: The column shows whether each onboarded resource has advanced security features on.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Overview of Microsoft Defender for Cloud DevOps security”, “Review your findings”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two prerequisites for the GitHub Advanced Security integration with Defender for Cloud?
notes.back: Any two of: a GitHub connector in Defender for Cloud, a GHAS licence, Defender CSPM on the subscription.
notes.explanation: Security Copilot is optional, for automated remediation.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “What is GitHub Advanced Security integration with Microsoft Defender for Cloud?”, “Availability and prerequisites”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: GitHub Advanced Security integration with Defender for Cloud

notes.front: A security team sees a vulnerable container running in production and wants to know which GitHub repository and code owner it came from. Which capability answers this?
notes.choices:
A) Dependabot version updates
B) Code-to-runtime mapping from the GHAS integration with Defender for Cloud
C) Push protection for users
D) The dependency review action
notes.back: B) Code-to-runtime mapping from the GHAS integration with Defender for Cloud
notes.choicesExplained: A updates dependencies, it does not trace workloads. C stops secrets being pushed. D compares dependencies within a pull request.
notes.explanation: The integration traces runtime vulnerabilities back to the originating repository and code owner.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “What is GitHub Advanced Security integration with Microsoft Defender for Cloud?”, “Automatic code-to-runtime mapping”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: GitHub Advanced Security integration with Defender for Cloud

notes.front: What are two runtime risk factors Defender for Cloud uses to prioritise GHAS findings?
notes.back: Any two of: internet exposure, sensitive data, critical resources, lateral movement.
notes.explanation: They come from Defender CSPM attack-path analysis of the running workload.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “What is GitHub Advanced Security integration with Microsoft Defender for Cloud?”, “Production-aware alert prioritization”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: GitHub Advanced Security integration with Defender for Cloud
